aliases.name: 女郎蜘蛛
aliases.meaning: 'Whore spider' or 'woman spider', the entomological / vernacular spelling

aliases.name: Jorō spider
aliases.meaning: Trichonephila clavata, the golden silk orb-weaver — the real spider lending its name to the yokai

description.summary: The Jorōgumo is a spider yōkai of Japanese folklore, traditionally said to be a Trichonephila clavata that has lived for centuries and gained the power to take the form of a beautiful woman, luring men to ensnare and devour. Famous as the haunt of Jōren Falls in the Izu Peninsula.
description.full: The Jorōgumo is a class of spider yōkai (妖怪) in Japanese folklore. The kanji 絡新婦 (literally 'entangling bride / newlywed') is the literary form; the homophonous 女郎蜘蛛 ('woman spider' or 'whore spider') is used in everyday and entomological writing for the real-world golden silk orb-weaver Trichonephila (formerly Nephila) clavata. Folk and Edo-period literary sources describe the Jorōgumo as a spider that, having lived for several hundred years, gains supernatural powers including the ability to transform into a beautiful woman, control her silk threads, and (in some accounts) breathe fire and command smaller fire-breathing spiders. She lures men — typically itinerant samurai, woodcutters, or travelers — to isolated waterfalls, mountain pools, or empty houses, plays seductive music (often the biwa), and binds them in supernaturally strong silk before consuming them. The most famous regional legend places her at the Jōren Falls (浄蓮の滝) on the Izu Peninsula in Shizuoka Prefecture, where a woodcutter is said to have escaped after being warned never to speak of what he saw — a vow he eventually breaks at his own peril. Major early literary sources are the Edo-period kaidan collections Tonoigusa (1660, by Ogita Ansei) and Taihei Hyakumonogatari (1732, anonymous), and Toriyama Sekien's illustrated bestiary Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (画図百鬼夜行, 1776), which depicts the Jorōgumo manipulating fire-breathing spiders. The figure remains a fixture of modern Japanese horror, manga (e.g. xxxHolic), anime, and video games.

etymology.origin: Japanese; the literary spelling 絡新婦 ('entangling new bride') puns on the homophonous 女郎蜘蛛 ('woman / courtesan spider'), the everyday name of the real Trichonephila clavata orb-weaver
etymology.first_use: Edo-period kaidan literature: Tonoigusa (1660); Taihei Hyakumonogatari (1732); Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776)

taxonomy.subtype: Animal-yokai with shapeshifting and femme-fatale aspects

coloration: true form: yellow-and-black-banded golden silk orb-weaver (Trichonephila clavata)
human form: pale-skinned, traditionally beautiful Edo-period woman

features.description: Body and patterning of a giant Trichonephila clavata, the golden silk orb-weaver, with characteristic yellow and black banding
Upon reaching several hundred years (commonly given as 400 in modern retellings), the spider gains the ability to transform into a beautiful young woman
Binds victims in silk threads strong enough to restrain humans
In Toriyama Sekien's depiction (Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, 1776), the Jorōgumo manipulates small fire-breathing spiders

physical.morphology: True form: large orb-weaving spider (Araneae: Araneidae). Disguise form: a woman in Edo-period attire.

abilities.description: Transformation from spider to beautiful woman
Spinning of supernaturally strong silk to immobilize victims
Plays the biwa (Japanese lute) or sings to draw victims into isolation

patterns: Targets isolated male travelers — woodcutters, samurai, monks
Often issues warnings or extracts secrecy oaths from would-be victims who escape

range.description: Native to Japanese folklore, with regional legends concentrated in central and western Honshu, especially the Izu Peninsula (Shizuoka), Kashikobuchi (Sendai, Miyagi), and the mountain forests of Kyoto and Kii.

hotspots.name: Jōren Falls (浄蓮の滝)

location.description: Waterfall on the Kano River, Izu Peninsula, Shizuoka Prefecture

hotspots.notes: Most famous regional legend: a woodcutter caught at the falls is bound by a Jorōgumo's web around his leg and barely escapes; the woodcutter's vow of secrecy and its breaking is the canonical narrative.

hotspots.name: Kashikobuchi (賢淵)

location.description: A pool on the Hirose River in Sendai, Miyagi Prefecture

hotspots.notes: Site of a Jorōgumo legend in which the spider is foiled by Buddhist intervention.

peak_activity_periods.description: Codification of the Jorōgumo legend in kaidan literature and Sekien's bestiary
Strong revival in manga, anime, video games, and horror cinema

origins.cultural_roots: Edo-period Japanese kaidan (怪談) ghost-story tradition; develops earlier medieval spider-yokai motifs (notably the tsuchigumo) into a femme-fatale shapeshifter.
origins.earliest_accounts: Ogita Ansei's Tonoigusa (1660) is among the earliest literary sources; Taihei Hyakumonogatari (1732) and Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (1776) are the canonical Edo-period sources.
origins.folklore_connections: Continuous with the broader Japanese spider-yokai tradition (tsuchigumo) and the regional waterfall- and mountain-spirit traditions of central Honshu.

timeline.event: Ogita Ansei's kaidan collection Tonoigusa (宿直草) records an early Jorōgumo tale
Anonymous publication of Taihei Hyakumonogatari (太平百物語), containing Jorōgumo stories
Toriyama Sekien publishes Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (画図百鬼夜行), illustrating the Jorōgumo with fire-breathing spider attendants
timeline.significance: Most influential Edo-period image of the Jorōgumo

history.modern_era: The Jorōgumo is a recurring fixture of Japanese horror and fantasy media, appearing in CLAMP's xxxHolic, Inuyasha, Nurarihyon no Mago, the Yo-kai Watch franchise, and numerous video games (Nioh, Onmyoji).

documentary.name: Tonoigusa (宿直草)
documentary.description: Early Edo-period kaidan collection by Ogita Ansei, including a Jorōgumo tale.

documentary.name: Taihei Hyakumonogatari (太平百物語)
documentary.description: Anonymous Edo-period 'hundred tales' collection containing Jorōgumo stories.

documentary.name: Gazu Hyakki Yagyō (画図百鬼夜行)
documentary.description: Toriyama Sekien's illustrated bestiary, depicting the Jorōgumo as a spider-woman attended by fire-breathing spiders.

paranormal.name: Animal-yokai 'aged-into-power' tradition
paranormal.description: Within Japanese folk thought, animals (foxes, tanuki, cats, spiders) that live to great age may acquire supernatural powers including shapeshifting; the Jorōgumo is a canonical instance for spiders.
evidence_cited: Continuity with kitsune, tanuki, and bakeneko traditions
Codification in Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō

skeptical.name: Cultural-folkloric figure
skeptical.description: The Jorōgumo is straightforwardly understood as a folkloric and literary creation, with the wordplay between 絡新婦 ('entangling bride') and 女郎蜘蛛 ('whore-spider', the real Trichonephila clavata) supplying its imaginative substrate.

stories: Toriyama Sekien's depiction of fire-breathing spider attendants
folklore.beliefs: Treated in modern Japan as canonical folklore rather than living belief; remains a beloved figure of regional tourism (Jōren Falls) and popular culture.

literature: CLAMP — xxxHolic (manga, 2003–2011) — features a Jorōgumo character
Lafcadio Hearn — references in Japanese ghost-tale collections
games: Shin Megami Tensei series — recurring demon
other: Jōren Falls regional tourism and signage
